"Sunny Afternoon" was first written in Ray Davies' house when he was sick.

"I'd bought a white upright piano. I hadn't written for a time. I'd been ill. I was living in a very 1960s-decorated house. It had orange walls and green furniture. My one-year-old daughter was crawling on the floor and I wrote the opening riff. I remember it vividly. I was wearing a polo-neck sweater".

Davies said of the song's lyrics, "The only way I could interpret how I felt was through a dusty, fallen aristocrat who had come from old money as opposed to the wealth I had created for myself." In order to prevent the listener from sympathizing with the song's protagonist, Davies said, "I turned him into a scoundrel who fought with his girlfriend after a night of drunkenness and cruelty."

Davies said of the song as well as its recording:

"Sunny Afternoon was made very quickly, in the morning, it was one of our most atmospheric sessions. I still like to keep tapes of the few minutes before the final take, things that happen before the session. Maybe it's superstitious, but I believe if I had done things differently — if I had walked around the studio or gone out—it wouldn't have turned out that way. The bass player went off and started playing funny little classical things on the bass, more like a lead guitar: and Nicky Hopkins, who was playing piano on that session, was playing "Liza"—we always used to play that song—little things like that helped us get into the feeling of the song.

At the time I wrote Sunny Afternoon I couldn't listen to anything. I was only playing The Greatest Hits of Frank Sinatra and Dylan's Maggie's Farm — I just liked its whole presence, I was playing the Bringing It All Back Home LP along with my Frank Sinatra and Glenn Miller and Bach —it was a strange time. I thought they all helped one another, they went into the chromatic part that's in the back of the song. I once made a drawing of my voice on Sunny Afternoon. It was a leaf with a very thick outline—a big blob in the background—the leaf just cutting through it".

It's an iceberg that no one saw coming. That puts to the test, sometimes violently, in the families of left, values ​​which seemed anchored for the life. An intimate torn, a rite of passage citizen and political, the first major opportunity, often, to confront his actions to his political speech. The eldest enters sixth.

Those who faced it had left to gentrify the popular districts, they had moved away from the city center because the real estate was no longer accessible there, they liked to cross their neighbors of origin and various social class on the Sunday morning at the market. They now understand that living in the neighborhood, in this suburb, is also to grow children together. But the public college sector has a bad reputation. In the charts of the best colleges, it is not as good as that of the block of houses next door. From year to year, college students do not really reflect the diversity of the neighborhood. Sometimes, it has become a "ghetto college", so many parents have already preferred to avoid it to their children. In dinners with friends, in families and within the couple, the discussions are strained. Then there is this sentence that summarizes everything: "The social mix will not be done on the back of my daughter!" A cry of despair that the philosopher Patrick Savidan understands well: "Because he did not take seriously the problem of coeducation at school, the state puts parents on notice to choose between their child and solidarity. " In September, a forum published in Libération , " To my friends who cheat with the school map ", had many reactions, both from "cheaters" and from parents who are angry at the small arrangements of their neighbors.

How to articulate, in the deepest of oneself, this decision not to educate one's child in the district, when one claimed in primary of the secular spirit of the school of the Republic, and that one was elected representatives FCPE with the school councils? How to justify daily this big difference between saying it ("I think it is important that everyone agrees to fight against inequalities") and do it ("I prefer to guarantee my child a reassuring inter-self")?

The death in the soul

Some parents, lucid, assume to have mourned some convictions and explain, without pride but without pretense, have established, death in the soul, a priority: my child is worth more than my principles. Others try to square the circle and plead the particular case. The youngest is too fragile. The older one took a sudden passion for the tuba ... that falls well, the famous college next door proposes a wind instruments option. Or, more political version: "As long as the private will not be forced to play the game of coeducation, no reason that I do (and in the meantime, I put my child in the said private). Between words, it is about being convinced that one is always left. Always think "well". "Parents who have always played the game of the public and mixed end up in some neighborhoods face a Corelian choice - ghetto or private - because of a lack of coordination of the public power, says Julien Grenet, teacher at the Paris School of Economics, which took part in the multisectorisation project set up last September in Paris to break some school ghettos. You can not blame them for saying no. What is shocking is that some parents, very intellectually armed, are blind and deny segregation with false arguments. "

It is often necessary that the subject arrives in the public square to be aware of its contradictions... in the eyes of others. Philippe Darriulat, assistant PS for school affairs of the city hall of the eighteenth (district) is constantly confronted. Between the chic avenue Junot and the social difficulties of the Montmartre gate, the district is undoubtedly, in Paris, the one where the big gap is the clearest. As a result, any modification, even marginal, of the school map becomes almost traumatic. "When I wanted to send 30 rather favored students across the boulevard Barbès because their institution was full, it was the jerk of battle and the judicial threats. The parents finally alerted the press, and there, boomerang effect. They understood that their fight was not so consensual ... " In their fight to want the best for their children, they had not perceived that this time, in the eyes of theirs, they were not good side.

"Contradictory injunctions"

"Parents are caught in a web of contradictory injunctions. They are not selfish or bad citizens. But they now decide in favor of a limited solidarity, intergenerational solidarity in favor of their child, to the detriment of a public solidarity ", analyzes Patrick Savidan, who dedicated a book to these terrible choices, Do we really want equality? (Albin Michel, 2015): how is it that in France, where the passion for equality is real, we opt for choices (bypassing the school map, "optimize" its taxes ...) that widen disparities Social? The philosopher, professor of political philosophy at the University Paris-Est - Créteil and president of the Observatory of inequalities, has a nice word to sum up these bad choices: the akrasia. "In philosophy, since antiquity, it is a weakness of the will. (YEAH RIGHT HAHA) Act contrary to what we know to be the best. It's not really immoral, not really irrational, it's the result of a contradictory injunction. It would be too easy to say that parents are hypocrites. The important question is: why? "

The obsession with "good choice" (as opposed to shit choice eh)

The avoidance practices and the resulting internal rifts exploded in the 90s, in peripheral suburban areas, according to geographer Michel Lussault, former president of the Higher Council of Programs (CSP). "The bourgeois circles, they had already long been used to send their children in the private, says the researcher. Gradually, the phenomenon will affect the salaried middle classes of the suburbs and big cities, like Paris or Lyon, which, historically, were at the base of the social pact in the French way and which brought their voice to the left in the name of the values " The lack of mixed institutions is not due, initially, to parents, but to the strategies of the state, says the geographer. "The city's policy has specialized certain territories in the reception of disadvantaged populations. Colleges and schools have become homogenized and segregated. " By their strategy of flight, parents have only accentuated the movement ... The problem is that these individual choices have, in turn, produced a collective situation. disastrous. Segregation today has become so entrenched in schools that we have less and less conscience to participate. "Nursery schools are still very mixed, says Julien Grenet. But every year, during primary school, there is a small loss. And at the entrance to the college, it bugue.

In all circles now, whether they opt for the private Catholic or Montessori school, making the "right choice" for the future of their child has become an obsession. Even more since unemployment has become massive. "School is considered the last insurance against the disappointments of professional life, reports Michel Lussault. A tool for maintaining social status, in a context of fierce struggle to reach the best places. " Each parent becomes a strategic entrepreneur, and families submit their beliefs and values ​​to the need to make their child succeed. They are not totally wrong: France is still the European country where the diploma is the most decisive element to enter the job market, but also for his entire career, as recalled Patrick Savidan: " Families no longer consider the state as a reliable or effective partner. In contrast to the 1960s, they feel that their efforts in the service of the community will not be at the same level. They prefer to take back the levers of solidarity and to reorient them towards their child by investing in private or support courses. "

At the heart of the choice of the tortured parents - and at the top of their justifications - the argument of the school level has sometimes given way to that of the emotional security and the psychological integrity of the child. The child has become an "overarching value, sacralised", comments Michel Lussault. It is no longer conceivable today that a child comes into tears from school because a big bothered him: "The slightest academic annoyance justifies avoidance," he regrets.

"Besieged Fortress"

Now that the vicious cycle of school avoidance is running at full speed, "the idea that it is normal to privilege the inter-sequent has become dominant," says the geographer. Parents often live the reintroduction projects of the mixed race in the mode of the besieged fortress. "

However, despite the representations conveyed in the collective imagination, diversity is not necessarily the ghetto. Filigree, it is undoubtedly another question that taunts the most torn parents: that of racism, at least social. "In this inter-self that we want to privilege, there is an obvious racial dimension," notes Michel Lussault bluntly. "A tendency to fall back, yes, a fear of the other probably, but racism, not really," nuance Philippe Darriulat. Much of school avoidance is based on representations, images and fantasies. "We try to avoid certain social groups deemed harmful, says Patrick Savidan. Everyone wants the social elevator, but not for the one on the floor below. In all these fears, there may be racism. But basically, there's no need to be racist to be part of this growing segregation. "

Do not be generous on your own

Playing on moral fiber will not be enough to progress on the path of school diversity. No doubt it will be necessary to accept that parents will play the game of the school map only if it benefits them: disadvantaged colleges even better endowed, very light classes, bonus for the assignment in high school, rare options dispensed primarily in the abandoned institutions (read opposite) ... One way to accept that the collective interest, if it wants to progress, must speak to the particular interest.

Very involved in the bisectorisation between the colleges Coysevox (rather not badly off) and Berlioz (more difficult) in the eighteenth in Paris, Philippe Darriulat was often faced with the anxiety, even anger, parents. "We can say what we want, what has the most weight, it is the word of the parents and the children who played the game. It is the peer-to-peer speech, the most useful. Not that of the expert, nor that of politics. "

Nobody wants to be generous alone. Parental associations, like in Paris, Learning Together (see opposite), try to make other arguments: to experience a school that is diverse and less disconnected from social realities can be an asset, even more later on the labor market. If families play the game together, nobody is a loser: a way to solve the prisoner's famous dilemma.
